question: Under Civil Code Section 1950.5 as amended by AB 12, what is the maximum security deposit most California landlords may charge for a rental unit, effective for deposits collected on or after July 1, 2024?
choice_a: Two months' rent for unfurnished units and three months' rent for furnished units, with no cap for furnished units
choice_b: There is no maximum security deposit under California law
choice_c: A flat $500 regardless of the rent amount
choice_d: An amount not exceeding one month's rent, regardless of whether the unit is furnished or unfurnished
explanation: AB 12 amended Civil Code Section 1950.5 to cap most landlords' security deposits at one month's rent for deposits collected on or after July 1, 2024, replacing the prior rule that allowed up to two months (unfurnished) or three months (furnished).
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5, as amended by AB 12 (2023), effective July 1, 2024

question: AB 12's one-month security deposit cap includes a narrower exception allowing a deposit of up to two months' rent for which landlords?
choice_a: A natural person or an LLC composed entirely of natural persons who owns no more than two residential rental properties totaling no more than four dwelling units
choice_b: Any landlord who owns more than 100 rental units statewide
choice_c: Only landlords renting to corporate tenants
choice_d: Only landlords located in San Francisco
explanation: AB 12 carves out a limited exception for small-scale landlords, natural persons or LLCs made up entirely of natural persons owning no more than two properties with a combined total of four units, who may still collect up to two months' rent as a deposit.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5(c), AB 12 small-landlord exception

question: Since AB 12, how must a landlord treat a request for a pet deposit on a rental unit?
choice_a: A landlord may always charge a separate pet deposit on top of the security deposit cap, without limit
choice_b: A pet deposit is considered part of the overall security deposit and must fit within the single security deposit cap, not charged as a separate additional deposit
choice_c: Pet deposits are entirely prohibited in California under all circumstances
choice_d: Pet deposits may only be collected in cash, never as part of a security deposit
explanation: AB 12 clarified that a pet deposit counts toward, rather than adds to, the capped security deposit amount, closing off the practice of stacking a separate pet deposit on top of the general deposit limit.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5, AB 12 pet deposit treatment

question: After a tenant vacates, how many days does a landlord have under Civil Code Section 1950.5 to return the security deposit or provide an itemized statement of deductions?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 10 days
choice_c: 21 days
choice_d: There is no statutory deadline
explanation: Civil Code Section 1950.5 requires a landlord to refund the security deposit, less any lawful deductions accompanied by an itemized written statement (and receipts for repairs over $125, in most cases), within 21 days after the tenant vacates.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5(g)

question: Under Civil Code Section 1954, absent an emergency, how much advance notice must a landlord generally give a tenant before entering a rental unit?
choice_a: No notice is legally required for a residential landlord to enter
choice_b: One week's advance notice for any entry
choice_c: 48 hours' notice, but only if requested by the tenant
choice_d: 24 hours' written notice, entering only at a reasonable time
explanation: Civil Code Section 1954 generally requires a landlord to provide at least 24 hours' written notice before entering, for statutorily permitted purposes such as repairs, showings, or inspections, and to enter only during reasonable hours.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1954

question: Under Civil Code Section 1946.1, how much notice must a landlord give to terminate the tenancy of a resident who has lived in the unit for one year or more, absent just cause under the Tenant Protection Act (where applicable)?
choice_a: 60 days' written notice
choice_b: 30 days' written notice, identical to shorter-term tenants
choice_c: No notice is required after one year of tenancy
choice_d: 90 days' written notice
explanation: For a periodic tenancy of one year or more, Civil Code Section 1946.1 generally requires 60 days' notice to terminate, compared to 30 days' notice for tenancies of less than one year, subject to additional just-cause requirements under the statewide Tenant Protection Act where it applies.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1946.1

question: Under the statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), what is the general cap on annual rent increases for covered residential tenancies?
choice_a: A flat 3% cap with no CPI adjustment
choice_b: The lesser of 10% or 5% plus the applicable regional CPI increase, over a 12-month period
choice_c: No cap at all; landlords may raise rent by any amount for covered units
choice_d: A flat 25% cap regardless of inflation
explanation: AB 1482 caps rent increases for covered units at 5% plus the local CPI increase, not to exceed 10% total in any 12-month period, and requires 'just cause' for most terminations of tenancies that have lasted 12 months or more.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1947.12, Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482)

question: Which category of rental property is commonly exempted from AB 1482's statewide rent cap, provided the landlord gives the tenant the statutorily required written notice of the exemption?
choice_a: All apartment buildings built before 1995
choice_b: Any unit rented to a tenant earning above the area median income
choice_c: Single-family homes and condominiums not owned by a real estate investment trust, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, when the required exemption notice is given
choice_d: Units located within one mile of a school
explanation: AB 1482 exempts certain single-family homes and condos from its rent cap and just-cause provisions (subject to ownership-structure limits and a required written exemption disclosure), along with other categories such as newer construction and certain owner-occupied duplexes.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1947.12, AB 1482 exemptions

question: Under AB 1482's just-cause eviction provisions, when a landlord terminates a qualifying tenancy for a 'no-fault' reason (such as an owner move-in or removing the unit from the rental market), what must generally be provided to the tenant?
choice_a: No compensation of any kind is required for a no-fault termination
choice_b: A rent increase in lieu of relocation assistance
choice_c: A cash payment equal to twelve months' rent
choice_d: Relocation assistance equal to one month's rent, or a rent waiver of the final month, along with proper notice
explanation: For a no-fault just-cause termination under AB 1482, covered landlords generally must provide relocation assistance equal to one month's rent (either as a direct payment or a waiver of the final month's rent), in addition to giving proper notice.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1946.2, AB 1482 relocation assistance for no-fault terminations

question: Under California's implied warranty of habitability (Civil Code Sections 1941 and 1941.1), a landlord has what basic obligation regarding a residential rental unit?
choice_a: To maintain the premises in a condition fit for human occupancy, addressing conditions such as effective waterproofing, working plumbing, heating, and electrical systems
choice_b: Only to ensure the unit has a working doorbell
choice_c: To repaint the unit annually regardless of condition
choice_d: No habitability obligation exists in California; habitability is purely a matter of lease negotiation
explanation: California law implies a warranty of habitability in every residential lease, obligating the landlord to maintain the property in a livable condition covering structural, plumbing, heating, electrical, and sanitation basics, among other statutory standards.
source_note: Civil Code Sections 1941, 1941.1; implied warranty of habitability

question: If a landlord fails to make necessary repairs after proper notice, what self-help remedy does Civil Code Section 1942 give a residential tenant?
choice_a: The tenant may withhold all future rent permanently with no further obligation
choice_b: The tenant may repair the defect and deduct the reasonable cost from rent, subject to statutory dollar and frequency limits
choice_c: The tenant must always sue in small claims court before taking any action
choice_d: The tenant has no remedy other than moving out
explanation: The 'repair and deduct' remedy under Civil Code Section 1942 allows a tenant, after proper notice to the landlord, to have necessary repairs made and deduct the cost from rent, subject to limits on the amount and how often the remedy can be used.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1942, repair-and-deduct remedy

question: In an unlawful detainer action for nonpayment of rent, what is the typical first statutory step a landlord must take before filing suit?
choice_a: Immediately change the locks on the unit without notice
choice_b: File criminal charges against the tenant for nonpayment
choice_c: Serve the tenant with a written 3-day notice to pay rent or quit the premises
choice_d: Wait a minimum of one year before taking any legal action
explanation: Before filing an unlawful detainer lawsuit for nonpayment of rent, a landlord must generally serve a written notice, most often a 3-day notice to pay rent or quit, giving the tenant the statutory opportunity to cure the default before litigation begins.
source_note: Code of Civil Procedure Section 1161, unlawful detainer notice requirements

question: Self-help eviction, such as a landlord changing the locks or shutting off utilities to force a tenant out without a court order, is treated under California law as what?
choice_a: A perfectly legal shortcut a landlord may use instead of the unlawful detainer process
choice_b: Legal only if the tenant is more than 30 days delinquent
choice_c: Legal only for commercial tenancies, never residential
choice_d: Illegal, exposing the landlord to statutory penalties and civil liability, regardless of whether the tenant is behind on rent
explanation: California law prohibits self-help evictions; a landlord must use the judicial unlawful detainer process to remove a tenant, and violating this prohibition, such as by lockouts or utility shutoffs, can expose the landlord to statutory damages.
source_note: Civil Code Section 789.3, prohibition on landlord self-help remedies

question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act as applied in California, how must a landlord treat a tenant's request for an assistance animal needed because of a disability?
choice_a: As a reasonable accommodation request that generally must be granted, and the assistance animal is not treated as a 'pet' subject to pet fees or deposits
choice_b: As an optional courtesy the landlord may deny for any reason, since assistance animals are treated exactly like ordinary pets
choice_c: As grounds to immediately terminate the tenancy
choice_d: As a request that automatically voids the lease
explanation: A legitimate assistance animal is a reasonable accommodation for a disability, not a pet, so a landlord generally cannot deny the request, charge a pet fee or deposit for the animal, or apply a no-pets policy to it.
source_note: Federal Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation requirements; California Fair Employment and Housing Act

question: When a real estate broker acts as a property manager for an owner-client, what is the broker's basic role regarding the relationship with the owner?
choice_a: An independent principal with no accountability to the property owner
choice_b: A fiduciary agent, owing the owner duties of care, loyalty, and accounting, while managing the property under a written property management agreement
choice_c: A neutral party with no fiduciary duty to either the owner or the tenants
choice_d: An employee of the tenant, not the owner
explanation: A broker managing property for an owner acts as the owner's fiduciary agent under a written management agreement, subject to standard agency duties including accounting for rents collected and acting in the owner's best interest.
source_note: General agency law principles applied to property management; DRE Reference Book, Property Management

question: A California property management agreement between a broker and an owner should typically specify which of the following essential terms?
choice_a: Only the tenant's name and phone number
choice_b: Nothing in writing is required for a valid property management relationship
choice_c: The scope of the broker's management authority, the management fee, the term of the agreement, and the broker's duties regarding rent collection and trust fund handling
choice_d: Only the make and model of the property's HVAC system
explanation: A well-drafted property management agreement spells out the broker's scope of authority, compensation, term, and specific duties, including how rents and deposits will be handled as trust funds, protecting both the owner and the broker.
source_note: DRE Reference Book, Property Management chapter; general management agreement essentials

question: Federal law generally requires what specific disclosure for the sale or lease of residential housing built before 1978?
choice_a: A disclosure about the age of the water heater only
choice_b: No federal disclosure is required for pre-1978 housing
choice_c: A disclosure exclusively about asbestos in attic insulation
choice_d: A lead-based paint disclosure, including any known information about lead-based paint hazards and a lead hazard information pamphlet
explanation: Federal law requires sellers and landlords of pre-1978 housing to disclose known lead-based paint hazards and provide an EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet, given the health risks associated with lead paint in older housing stock.
source_note: Federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992 (Title X); 24 CFR Part 35 / 40 CFR Part 745

question: California law requires that residential lease and rental agreements include a notice referencing what public information resource, related to registered sex offenders?
choice_a: The Megan's Law database maintained by the California Department of Justice
choice_b: The California DMV's driving record database
choice_c: The county assessor's property tax roll
choice_d: The federal no-fly list
explanation: California requires most residential leases and rental agreements to include a specific notice informing tenants about the Megan's Law database and how to access registered sex offender information.
source_note: Civil Code Section 2079.10a, Megan's Law lease notice requirement

question: If a rent increase for a non-exempt tenancy would raise the rent by more than 10% over a 12-month period, what notice period does Civil Code Section 827 generally require, in addition to any applicable AB 1482 cap?
choice_a: No notice is required for increases above 10%
choice_b: 90 days' advance written notice
choice_c: 10 days' notice
choice_d: Notice may be given verbally with no writing required
explanation: Civil Code Section 827 requires 90 days' notice for a rent increase exceeding 10% within a 12-month period (30 days' notice for increases of 10% or less), separate from and in addition to any percentage cap that may apply under the statewide Tenant Protection Act.
source_note: Civil Code Section 827, rent increase notice periods

question: A tenant who has resided in a unit for less than one year may generally have their periodic tenancy terminated by the landlord with how much notice, absent AB 1482 just-cause protection?
choice_a: 60 days' written notice, identical to longer-term tenants
choice_b: No notice is required for shorter-term tenants
choice_c: 30 days' written notice
choice_d: One year's notice
explanation: For tenancies under one year, Civil Code Section 1946.1 generally requires only 30 days' notice to terminate a periodic tenancy, compared to the 60-day notice required once a tenancy reaches one year or more.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1946.1

question: How does the broker exam's emphasis on landlord-tenant and property management law compare to that of the salesperson exam, and why?
choice_a: Landlord-tenant law is completely absent from both exams
choice_b: The salesperson exam tests landlord-tenant law far more heavily than the broker exam
choice_c: There is no difference at all, and the topic is weighted identically on both exams
choice_d: The broker exam tests this area in greater depth, since brokers more commonly manage income and rental properties and supervise property management activity under their license
explanation: Because a broker license is the credential most closely tied to running a brokerage that includes property management, the broker exam draws more heavily on landlord-tenant and property management topics within the shared DRE content outline's 'Practice of Real Estate' area.
source_note: DRE Examination Description RE 425 (Rev. 6/25), differing emphasis by license level

question: A California city or county may enact a local ordinance requiring landlords to do what regarding tenant security deposits, beyond the statewide minimum?
choice_a: Pay tenants annual interest on held security deposits, since some local jurisdictions impose this requirement even though state law does not require it statewide
choice_b: Nothing; local governments have no authority over any aspect of landlord-tenant relationships
choice_c: Eliminate the statewide 21-day deposit return deadline entirely
choice_d: Require deposits to be held in a foreign bank account
explanation: While state law does not require interest on security deposits statewide, several California cities have local rent ordinances that require landlords to pay tenants interest on deposits held for a certain period, illustrating how local law can add obligations beyond the statewide floor.
source_note: Local rent control/security deposit ordinances layered atop Civil Code Section 1950.5

question: What is the primary purpose of requiring a landlord to provide an itemized statement of security deposit deductions rather than simply keeping whatever portion the landlord deems appropriate?
choice_a: It exists only to create extra paperwork with no protective purpose
choice_b: It protects the tenant by requiring transparency and justification for each deduction, discouraging improper or excessive withholding of deposit funds
choice_c: It is required solely for the landlord's own tax records and has no benefit to the tenant
choice_d: It allows a landlord to withhold the deposit indefinitely as long as an itemization is eventually provided
explanation: The itemization requirement forces landlords to document the actual, reasonable basis for any deduction (such as unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear), which protects tenants from arbitrary or inflated withholding of deposit funds.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5, itemized deduction statement requirement

question: 'Normal wear and tear' on a rental unit is generally treated under California law as what, when a landlord considers deposit deductions?
choice_a: Always fully deductible from the tenant's security deposit, regardless of cause
choice_b: A criminal offense committed by the tenant
choice_c: A cost the landlord must absorb as a normal part of renting the property, not a deductible item from the tenant's security deposit
choice_d: Irrelevant, since landlords may deduct any amount they choose for any reason
explanation: Ordinary wear and tear, gradual deterioration from normal, expected use, is not chargeable to the tenant's deposit; only damage beyond normal use, unpaid rent, or cleaning needed to restore the unit to its move-in condition may be deducted.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5, permissible vs. impermissible deposit deductions

question: A broker managing a residential rental property on behalf of an out-of-state owner has what obligation regarding trust funds collected, such as rent and deposits?
choice_a: None; out-of-state owners' funds are exempt from California trust fund law
choice_b: The broker may treat the funds as personal income since the owner cannot easily monitor the account
choice_c: The three-business-day deposit rule does not apply because the owner is out of state
choice_d: The same trust fund deposit, accounting, and non-commingling obligations apply as with any other client, regardless of where the owner resides
explanation: California trust fund law applies based on the broker's license and the location of the transaction, not the owner's residency; an out-of-state owner is entitled to the same trust accounting protections as any California-based client.
source_note: Business and Professions Code Section 10145; trust fund obligations apply regardless of owner's residency

question: Under AB 1482's just-cause framework, what distinguishes an 'at-fault' just cause termination from a 'no-fault' just cause termination?
choice_a: An at-fault termination is based on tenant misconduct, such as nonpayment of rent or a lease violation, while a no-fault termination is based on landlord circumstances unrelated to tenant behavior, such as an owner move-in
choice_b: There is no legal distinction between the two categories
choice_c: At-fault terminations require relocation assistance, while no-fault terminations never do
choice_d: No-fault terminations are always illegal in California
explanation: At-fault just cause is tied to something the tenant did (such as nonpayment or breach of the lease), while no-fault just cause is based on circumstances not attributable to the tenant (such as the owner or a family member moving in, or removing the unit from the rental market), and generally only no-fault terminations trigger the relocation-assistance requirement.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1946.2, AB 1482 at-fault vs. no-fault just cause

question: A tenant subjected to substandard housing conditions, such as a serious plumbing or structural defect that a landlord has failed to remedy, may report the condition to which type of agency for enforcement?
choice_a: Only the DRE, since it is the sole agency with jurisdiction over housing conditions
choice_b: A local code enforcement or health department, which can inspect and cite the landlord under state housing and health and safety standards
choice_c: The IRS
choice_d: No agency has jurisdiction over housing conditions in California
explanation: Substandard housing conditions are typically enforced by local code enforcement or health departments under the State Housing Law and Health and Safety Code provisions on substandard buildings, separate from DRE's jurisdiction over real estate licensees.
source_note: Health and Safety Code Section 17920.3, substandard housing conditions; local code enforcement authority

question: Under Business and Professions Code Section 10131(b), which activity performed for another, for compensation, generally requires a California real estate license?
choice_a: Leasing or renting real property, soliciting listings of places for rent, negotiating leases, or collecting rents from real property on behalf of an owner
choice_b: Painting the interior of a rental unit between tenancies as an independent painting contractor
choice_c: Mowing the lawn of a rental property as a licensed landscaping contractor
choice_d: Delivering mail addressed to a rental property as a postal carrier
explanation: Business and Professions Code Section 10131(b) defines a real estate broker to include a person who, for compensation, leases or rents property, solicits rental listings or prospective tenants, negotiates leases, or collects rents on behalf of an owner, activities at the core of licensed property management.
source_note: Business and Professions Code Section 10131(b)

question: Which individual is exempt from real estate licensing requirements under Business and Professions Code Section 10131.01, despite performing day-to-day property management tasks?
choice_a: The resident manager of an apartment building, apartment complex, or court, and that manager's employees, with respect to their management of that property
choice_b: A broker managing dozens of rental properties for unrelated third-party owners across the county
choice_c: An unlicensed individual who manages properties for owners the individual has never met, in multiple counties
choice_d: An unlicensed individual who negotiates and signs leases on an owner's behalf for a fee
explanation: Business and Professions Code Section 10131.01 exempts a resident manager of an apartment building, complex, or court, along with that manager's employees, from real estate licensing requirements for their management activities at that property, recognizing the practical reality of on-site apartment management.
source_note: Business and Professions Code Section 10131.01, resident manager exemption

question: Under Civil Code Section 1941.3, which security devices must a landlord install and maintain on a residential rental unit?
choice_a: An operable dead bolt lock on each main swinging entry door and operable window security or locking devices on windows designed to be opened
choice_b: A monitored electronic burglar alarm system connected to a private security company in every unit
choice_c: Security cameras recording all common areas of the property
choice_d: No security devices are required by California statute
explanation: Civil Code Section 1941.3 requires a landlord to install and maintain an operable dead bolt lock on each main swinging entry door (extending at least 13/16 inch into the strike) and operable window security or locking devices on openable windows, subject to specified exemptions such as sliding doors and high windows.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1941.3, required security devices

question: Under Civil Code Section 1946.2, when a residential unit has multiple adult tenants who began occupying the unit at different times and not all of them have lived there for 12 months, when does just-cause eviction protection first apply?
choice_a: Once at least one of the tenants has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 24 months
choice_b: Just-cause protection never applies unless every tenant moved in on the exact same date
choice_c: Protection begins the day the newest tenant signs the lease, regardless of anyone's occupancy length
choice_d: Protection applies only if all of the tenants are related to one another
explanation: Under Civil Code Section 1946.2, if not all tenants have occupied the unit for 12 months, the tenancy is still covered once at least one tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 24 months, in addition to the baseline rule that protection applies once all tenants have occupied for 12 months.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1946.2, covered tenancy definition

question: Which of the following is listed as an 'at-fault' just cause for termination under Civil Code Section 1946.2?
choice_a: The tenant assigning or subletting the premises in violation of the tenant's lease
choice_b: The owner deciding to sell the property to a new buyer
choice_c: The owner wishing to raise the rent beyond what the statewide rent cap would otherwise allow
choice_d: The property needing routine, non-substantial repainting
explanation: Civil Code Section 1946.2 lists an unauthorized assignment or sublet in violation of the lease as one of the enumerated at-fault just causes for termination, alongside grounds such as nonpayment of rent, breach of a material lease term after notice to cure, nuisance, waste, and criminal activity on the property.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1946.2(b)(1), at-fault just cause

question: Under Civil Code Section 1946.2, once a landlord elects to pay relocation assistance in cash (rather than waiving the tenant's final month of rent) for a no-fault termination, when must that payment generally be made?
choice_a: Within 15 calendar days of service of the termination notice
choice_b: Within 90 days after the tenant has fully vacated
choice_c: At the same time the landlord files an unlawful detainer lawsuit
choice_d: There is no deadline; the landlord may pay at any time before trial
explanation: Civil Code Section 1946.2 requires that, if relocation assistance is paid directly rather than applied as a rent waiver for the final month, the payment must be made within 15 calendar days of service of the notice of termination.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1946.2(d)(1), relocation assistance timing

question: Under Civil Code Section 1950.5, if a tenant requests a pre-move-out inspection before vacating, when may the landlord conduct it and what must the landlord provide the tenant beforehand?
choice_a: No earlier than two weeks before the end of the tenancy, after giving the tenant at least 48 hours' prior written notice, so the tenant has an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies before the final move-out inspection
choice_b: The inspection may occur only after the tenant has already vacated and returned all keys
choice_c: The inspection must occur exactly six months before move-out, with no notice to the tenant required
choice_d: No advance notice of any kind is ever required for a pre-move-out inspection
explanation: Civil Code Section 1950.5 gives a tenant the right to request an initial pre-move-out inspection, which the landlord must conduct no earlier than two weeks before the end of the tenancy after providing at least 48 hours' written notice (unless both parties waive that notice), giving the tenant a chance to fix identified issues before final deposit deductions are calculated.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5(f), pre-move-out inspection right

question: Under Civil Code Section 1950.5, when a landlord deducts more than $125 from a tenant's security deposit for repair costs, what must the landlord generally provide along with the itemized statement of deductions?
choice_a: Copies of documents, such as the bill, invoice, or receipt, showing the charges actually incurred and deducted for the repair work
choice_b: Nothing further; the itemized statement alone is legally sufficient for any deduction amount
choice_c: A notarized affidavit prepared by the landlord's attorney
choice_d: A copy of the landlord's most recent federal income tax return
explanation: Civil Code Section 1950.5 requires that when itemized repair or cleaning deductions exceed $125 in total, the landlord must include copies of documents such as invoices, bills, or receipts substantiating the charges, unless a statutory exception applies (such as the work being performed by the landlord's own employee).
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5(g)(2), receipts for deductions over $125

question: If a rental property is sold and the prior landlord fails to properly transfer or account for a tenant's security deposit as Civil Code Section 1950.5 requires, what is the new owner's exposure?
choice_a: The new owner (successor landlord) can be held jointly and severally liable with the prior landlord for repayment of the security deposit
choice_b: The new owner bears no responsibility whatsoever for a deposit collected by the prior owner
choice_c: The tenant automatically and permanently forfeits the deposit once the property changes hands
choice_d: Only the real estate broker who handled the sale can ever be held liable, never the new owner
explanation: Civil Code Section 1950.5 makes a successor landlord jointly and severally liable with the prior landlord for repayment of the security deposit when the deposit was not properly transferred or accounted for upon the sale of the property, protecting the tenant's interest in the deposit through a change in ownership.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5, successor landlord liability for security deposits

question: What does the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act primarily do, as distinguished from the statewide AB 1482 rent cap?
choice_a: It preempts local (city or county) rent control ordinances from applying to certain categories of units, such as separately alienable single-family homes/condominiums and post-1995 new construction, whereas AB 1482 imposes a separate statewide cap on annual rent increases for covered units
choice_b: It is simply another name for AB 1482 and imposes an identical statewide rent-increase cap
choice_c: It abolishes all rent control, both local and state, throughout California
choice_d: It applies only to commercial leases and has no bearing on residential tenancies
explanation: The Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act is a state preemption statute limiting which units local rent control ordinances may cover, exempting categories such as separately alienable single-family homes/condos and certain new construction, and establishing vacancy decontrol; it is legally distinct from AB 1482's statewide percentage cap on rent increases.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1954.50 et seq., Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act

question: Under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, a dwelling unit that is 'alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit' (as most single-family homes and separately-sold condominiums are) is generally treated how with respect to LOCAL rent control ordinances?
choice_a: Exempt from local rent control, allowing the owner to set and increase rent under state law rather than a local ordinance's rent-setting rules, subject to any other applicable state protections such as AB 1482
choice_b: Subject to the strictest local rent control ordinance in the state, with no exemption available
choice_c: Automatically exempt from AB 1482 as well, in every case
choice_d: Left entirely unregulated, with neither state nor local law applying
explanation: Civil Code Section 1954.52 exempts dwelling units that are alienable separate from title to any other unit, such as most single-family homes and separately-sold condominiums, from local rent control ordinances, though such units may still be subject to separate statewide protections like AB 1482 where applicable.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1954.52(a)(3), Costa-Hawkins separately alienable unit exemption

question: Under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act's 'vacancy decontrol' principle, what may an owner generally do once a tenant voluntarily vacates a rent-controlled unit or is lawfully evicted?
choice_a: Establish the initial rental rate for the next tenancy without being bound by the prior tenant's local rent-controlled rate
choice_b: Nothing; the next tenant must be charged exactly the same rent the prior tenant paid, in every circumstance
choice_c: Automatically double the rent regardless of market conditions
choice_d: Refuse to re-rent the unit for a minimum of five years
explanation: Vacancy decontrol under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act allows an owner to set the initial rent for a new tenancy at market rate once the prior tenancy ends through voluntary vacancy or lawful eviction, rather than being locked into the previous tenant's local rent-controlled amount.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1954.53, Costa-Hawkins vacancy decontrol

question: Under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, a residential unit is generally exempt from local rent control based on new construction if it was issued a certificate of occupancy after what date?
choice_a: February 1, 1995
choice_b: January 1, 2020
choice_c: July 1, 2024
choice_d: There is no date-based new-construction exemption under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act
explanation: Civil Code Section 1954.52 exempts units first issued a certificate of occupancy after February 1, 1995 from local rent control ordinances, a fixed historical date distinct from AB 1482's separate, rolling 15-year new-construction exemption from the statewide rent cap.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1954.52(a)(1), Costa-Hawkins new construction exemption

question: Under Civil Code Section 1942.5, within how many days of a tenant's protected act (such as making a habitability complaint to a government agency or requesting repairs) is a landlord generally barred from retaliating by evicting the tenant, raising rent, or reducing services?
choice_a: 180 days
choice_b: 10 days
choice_c: 5 years
choice_d: There is no time-based retaliation protection under California statute
explanation: Civil Code Section 1942.5 creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if a landlord takes adverse action, such as eviction, a rent increase, or a reduction in services, within 180 days of a tenant's protected activity, such as a habitability complaint or repair request, though a tenant generally cannot invoke this presumption more than once in any 12-month period.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1942.5, retaliatory eviction presumption period

question: If a landlord is found to have retaliated against a tenant in violation of Civil Code Section 1942.5 with fraud, oppression, or malice, what remedy, beyond actual damages, may a court award?
choice_a: Statutory penalties of not less than $100 nor more than $2,000 for each retaliatory act, plus reasonable attorney's fees awarded to the prevailing party upon request
choice_b: Automatic criminal imprisonment of the landlord
choice_c: Forfeiture of the landlord's title to the property in favor of the tenant
choice_d: No additional remedy is available beyond the tenant's actual damages
explanation: Civil Code Section 1942.5 authorizes a court to award statutory penalties between $100 and $2,000 per retaliatory act where the landlord acted with fraud, oppression, or malice, on top of the tenant's actual damages, and the statute directs an award of reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party upon request.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1942.5, retaliatory eviction penalties

question: Under Civil Code Section 1954.603, what must a landlord provide to a prospective tenant before creating a new residential tenancy?
choice_a: A written notice, in at least 10-point type, containing general information about bed bug identification, behavior, common signs of infestation, and how to report a suspected infestation to the landlord
choice_b: A live demonstration of pest-control equipment at the leasing office
choice_c: Nothing; bed bug infestations are not addressed by California statute
choice_d: A notarized statement guaranteeing that the unit has never had a bed bug infestation
explanation: Civil Code Section 1954.603 requires landlords, before creating a new tenancy, to give prospective tenants a written notice (in at least 10-point type) covering bed bug identification, behavior, bite reactions, prevention cooperation, and how to report suspected infestations.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1954.603, bed bug disclosure requirement

question: Under Civil Code Section 1950.6, an application/tenant-screening fee charged to a rental applicant is limited to what?
choice_a: The landlord's actual out-of-pocket costs of screening the applicant, such as a credit or tenant-screening report, up to a statutory base cap of $30 that the landlord may adjust annually for the Consumer Price Index
choice_b: Whatever amount the rental market will bear, with no statutory limit at all
choice_c: A flat $1,000 fee, regardless of the landlord's actual screening costs
choice_d: Screening fees of any kind are entirely prohibited in California
explanation: Civil Code Section 1950.6 caps an application screening fee at the landlord's actual out-of-pocket cost of gathering applicant information (such as a screening or credit report and reasonable value of staff time), based on a statutory ceiling originally set at $30 that may be adjusted annually according to the Consumer Price Index, with unused portions refundable to the applicant.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.6, tenant screening/application fee cap

question: Under Health and Safety Code Section 13113.8, before transferring title to a single-family residential dwelling, what must the transferor (seller) provide regarding smoke alarms?
choice_a: A written statement that the transferor is in compliance with the statute's requirement that the dwelling have an operable smoke alarm
choice_b: Nothing; smoke alarm compliance is not addressed at the time of a residential sale under California law
choice_c: A signed waiver obtained from the local fire department
choice_d: Proof that the smoke alarms were installed exclusively by a licensed electrician
explanation: Health and Safety Code Section 13113.8 requires that every single-family dwelling sold have an operable smoke alarm, and the transferor must provide a written statement, delivered as soon as practicable before transfer of title, indicating compliance with this requirement.
source_note: Health and Safety Code Section 13113.8, smoke alarm compliance statement

question: Under Health and Safety Code Section 17926, an owner of a dwelling unit with a fossil fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage is generally required to install what device, and by when for existing single-family dwellings?
choice_a: A carbon monoxide detection device, with existing single-family dwellings required to have one installed on or before July 1, 2011
choice_b: A radon gas detector, with no installation deadline specified in the statute
choice_c: A natural gas leak detector, required only in commercial buildings, never in residential units
choice_d: No detection device of any kind is required under California law
explanation: Health and Safety Code Section 17926 required owners of dwelling units with a fossil fuel appliance, fireplace, or attached garage to install carbon monoxide detection devices, with a compliance deadline of on or before July 1, 2011 for existing single-family dwellings (later deadlines applied to other categories of existing dwellings and to hotels/motels).
source_note: Health and Safety Code Section 17926, carbon monoxide detector requirement

question: When a landlord claims an exemption from AB 1482's statewide rent cap and just-cause requirements (for example, under the qualifying single-family home/condo exemption or the owner-occupied duplex exemption), what must the landlord generally do?
choice_a: Include a specific written statement, either in the lease or in a separate notice, informing the tenant that the property is exempt from the rent limits of Civil Code Section 1947.12 and the just-cause requirements of Civil Code Section 1946.2, and that the owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member
choice_b: Nothing at all; qualifying exemptions apply automatically with no notice obligation whatsoever
choice_c: Provide only a verbal statement made at the moment of lease signing, with no written requirement
choice_d: File a notarized deed restriction with the county recorder's office before every new tenancy
explanation: To claim certain AB 1482 exemptions, such as for a qualifying single-family home/condo or an owner-occupied duplex, Civil Code Sections 1947.12 and 1946.2 require the landlord to provide the tenant a specific written exemption statement, including confirmation that the owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, or the exemption may not be enforceable.
source_note: Civil Code Sections 1947.12(g) and 1946.2, AB 1482 exemption notice requirement

question: Under Government Code Section 12955 (part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act), a landlord's refusal to rent to an otherwise-qualified applicant solely because the applicant intends to pay using a Section 8 housing choice voucher is generally treated as what?
choice_a: Unlawful discrimination based on source of income, since the statute's definition of protected 'source of income' expressly includes federal housing assistance vouchers issued under Section 8 of the United States Housing Act
choice_b: A permissible business decision carrying no legal consequence under California law
choice_c: An action affirmatively required of every landlord in every circumstance
choice_d: A matter relevant only to commercial leasing, with no application to residential rentals
explanation: Government Code Section 12955 prohibits housing discrimination based on 'source of income,' a term the statute expressly defines to include federal, state, or local housing subsidies such as Section 8 housing choice vouchers, making a categorical refusal to accept voucher-holders unlawful discrimination.
source_note: Government Code Section 12955, Fair Employment and Housing Act source-of-income protection

question: Besides nonpayment of rent, on what other basis may a landlord pursue an unlawful detainer action against a tenant who remains in possession of a rental unit?
choice_a: The tenant's holding over in possession after a properly served and expired termination notice (such as a 30-day or 60-day notice, or a notice based on an at-fault or no-fault just cause), so long as the landlord proceeds through the court process rather than self-help
choice_b: The landlord simply changing the locks while the tenant is temporarily away from the unit
choice_c: The landlord's mere preference for a higher-paying tenant, without any notice or judicial process
choice_d: Unlawful detainer is available only for nonpayment of rent and for no other reason
explanation: An unlawful detainer action is also available when a tenant holds over after a valid termination notice (such as a 30-day or 60-day notice, or a notice grounded in an at-fault or no-fault just cause under Civil Code Section 1946.2 where applicable) has properly expired, provided the landlord uses the court process rather than self-help.
source_note: Code of Civil Procedure Section 1161, unlawful detainer grounds beyond nonpayment

question: Under Civil Code Section 1954, in what situation may a landlord enter a rental unit without giving the tenant the ordinarily-required 24-hour written notice?
choice_a: In a genuine emergency
choice_b: Any time the landlord simply wants to check on the condition of the property
choice_c: Only if the tenant is more than 30 days late on rent
choice_d: Never; written notice is required in absolutely every circumstance, including emergencies
explanation: Civil Code Section 1954 excuses the ordinary 24-hour written notice requirement in a genuine emergency, recognizing that urgent situations such as a fire, flood, or major utility failure require a landlord to be able to enter immediately to protect the property and its occupants.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1954, emergency exception to entry notice

question: Under Civil Code Section 1950.5, the small-landlord exception permitting a security deposit of up to two months' rent applies to most otherwise-qualifying small landlords, but does NOT extend to which category of tenant?
choice_a: A tenant who is a servicemember, as defined under the statute
choice_b: A tenant who has a pet
choice_c: A tenant who pays rent monthly rather than weekly
choice_d: A tenant who has lived in the unit for more than five years
explanation: Civil Code Section 1950.5's small-landlord exception, allowing certain small-scale owners to collect up to two months' rent as a security deposit, does not apply where the tenant is a servicemember, so a servicemember-tenant remains subject to the standard one-month deposit cap even when renting from a qualifying small landlord.
source_note: Civil Code Section 1950.5(c), servicemember exception to small-landlord deposit exception
